primitives.name: Variational Bayes
primitives.verbatim_quote: Equations & assumptions Variational objective: ELBO = E_q[log p(y|w,x)] - KL(q(w)‖p(w)) with factorized Gaussian q.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'E_q': 'Expectation under variational posterior distribution, dimensionless', 'log p(y|w,x)': 'Log-likelihood of observed data given parameters, natural units', 'KL(q(w)‖p(w))': 'Kullback-Leibler divergence between variational posterior and prior, bits', 'q(w)': 'Mean-field Gaussian variational posterior over model weights, N-dimensional', 'p(w)': 'Prior distribution over model weights, N-dimensional'}
primitives.assumptions: Mean-field variational approximation assumes independent latent variables; Gaussian posterior factorization may underrepresent true weight correlations; ELBO maximization provides a lower bound on marginal likelihood.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs when variational posterior collapses to a point mass, violating the KL divergence term; also fails if true posterior has multiple modes that cannot be represented by a single Gaussian.

layer2.telemetry: Effective sample size of variational posterior vs. true posterior; predictive sharpness vs. calibration error on holdout data.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core challenge is distinguishing between intrinsic uncertainty from variational Bayes (VI) versus post-hoc calibration of point estimates. VI introduces stochasticity directly into the model parameters, yielding a distribution over predictions. In contrast, calibration methods adjust the output logits of a deterministic network to match marginal label frequencies, preserving the original point estimate while altering confidence scores. Empirically, VI can capture heteroscedastic noise or aleatoric uncertainty, whereas calibration primarily addresses miscalibration due to dataset shift or model bias. Both approaches reduce log-loss, but their failure modes differ: VI may over-smooth posteriors leading to overly confident predictions on easy examples, while calibration can fail catastrophically on out-of-distribution inputs if the calibration set lacks sufficient coverage. The average-rank result (BNN 2.0952 vs. isotonic 4.2857) suggests VI dominates on easier tasks, but the Wilcoxon test shows no statistical significance against beta and logistic, indicating that the BNN's edge is fragile and dataset-specific.
